body:
Base64 is a way to write arbitrary binary data using only printable text. IETF RFC 4648 describes it as representing sequences of 8-bit octets with a set of 65 human-readable ASCII characters: 64 that carry data and one, the equals sign, used for padding.

The method works on blocks of 24 bits, which is three 8-bit bytes. Each block is split into four groups of 6 bits. A 6-bit group can hold a number from 0 to 63, so each group selects exactly one position in a 64-character table. The standard table runs through the capital letters A to Z, then the lowercase letters a to z, then the digits 0 to 9, and finally the plus sign and the slash. Each 6-bit number is replaced by the character at that position, so every three bytes of input become four characters of output.

Data does not always divide evenly into three-byte blocks. When fewer than 24 bits remain at the end, zero bits are added to complete the final 6-bit group, and equals signs are written to show that bytes were missing from the last block.

This note covers only the standard alphabet and padding rule summarized above; the same RFC also defines Base16 and Base32, which are not described here.

summary: Base64 turns every three bytes of data into four characters from a 64-symbol table of A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9, plus and slash, with equals signs marking missing bytes at the end.
title: Write bytes as plain letters with Base64
